text:
At 3:12 every Thursday morning, I find the book in the bread rack.
Always the same one: The Practical Guide to Inland Birds, cracked blue spine, and a library stamp from a town forty miles away.
I'd set it on the flour bin, wipe the butter off the cover, and mean to return it after my shift.
By noon, the errands, heat, and sleep swallow the thought.
Then, next Thursday, there it is again, tucked between the cooling rye loaves.
Tonight the bakery hums with the proofing cabinet and the old radio's static.
Rain presses silver lines down the front window.
I lift the book with both hands, as if it might be warm.
A folded receipt marks the heron chapter.
I open it.
In block letters, someone had written: I THINK YOU ARE THE ONLY PERSON AWAKE WHEN I AM. PAGE 47.
I turn to page 47.
A grey heron stands in a marsh, one foot raised, patient as a saint.
Under the picture, in pencil, is the note: THURSDAY, 3:30?
The clock over the mixer clicks once.
I brush the flour off my apron, unlock the front door, and turn on the little OPEN sign.
